Cites Elephants

By: Johann Botha | Production

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Cites ended this week and the rules of trade in endangered were set for the next three years. Where does it leave South Africa?

Unique Selling Point:
Footage of elephant poaching in Central Africa
Interviews with main governments and environmentalists involved in global elephant conservation

Summary:
Elephant range states are split in two groups. The Northern states, Kenia, Tanzania, Gabon, Cameroon etc have the larger area but have fewer elephants and do not have the infrastructure to protect them against poachers. Since 1989 all their elephants were listed on Cites appendix1, meaning no international trade at all in elephant products. Since 2008 they've lost thousands of elephants to increased syndicated and military poaching. They are pushing to now move the southern countries elephants also to appendix1, as they feel that ivory sales from the southern countries stimulated the market and caused the current upsurge in poaching in their elephant populations.
The southern range states are pushing to keep their elephants on appendix 2 and are asking permission to be allowed to sell their stockpiles to generate funds for local communities who are suffering crop losses etc. The whole debate is coming to a head on monday this week and with the final voting on wednesday.

Press Release:


Saving the Elephant
To trade or to ban trading? The CITES COP17 conference ended this week, with several key decisions made to curb the illegal trade in endangered species. But despite vehement debate, rules banning the sale of ivory remain unchanged and for Africa’s rapidly dwindling elephant numbers, the next three years could be a tipping point as elephant poaching continues unabated. Carte Blanche asks: has the ban on ivory sales proven a complete failure or is it still key to the future survival of the species?


Script:


Bongani It seems obvious enough, but the thing about elephants is, well, they're big, and they need space. You can't just throw them into a reserve and think you've conserved them. And, as the human population continues to explode, the competition for the space is going to get more fierce with every year.
From a safe distance, we are in awe by their sheer size, intelligence and grace. Living between them, especially unarmed, is another story. This family, in South Luanga in Zambia just lost their whole years' staple food in one night.
Crop damage man From there, unto there, its an elephant destroy it
" And you''l find families like this just about everywhere where you find wild elephants.
Far from this reality, at the glamorous Cites conference in Sandton, the big debate was once again, around elephants. To secure their future, one side believes you have to sell their ivory, while the other side believes you can only save them by burning the ivory stockpiles. "
"Philip Muruthi
AWF" Do not inject more ivory into the market at this time because it's going to cause more poaching. Deal with the crisis.
Pohamba Namibian minister of environment It is very difficult to live with these animals. You'll experience daily this excruciating conflict with animals. They are wild, this is not animals in a zoo
Killing the mighty elephant has always been proof of man's dominance over the beasts, and that's why ivory became such a sought after status symbol. And so the slaughtering and the trade began, centuries ago. Today the biggest market is in China, and Viet Nam but as Tom points out, it is a cycle which starts when a country has a sudden growing middle class. America, England and Japan have all at one stage or another been the major importers of ivory.
Tom on middle class symbols Every time that we get a country that has some sort of historical relationship with the ivory trade, and suddenly their... the makeup of the society, the disposable wealth in society has brought affluence to a large number of people who now want to show status - we will see an ivory trade. And that is where China is now.
"Because of this demand, elephants are also soft targets fro armed forces looking to fund their wars.
The South African government and the rebel group Unita slaughtered whole herds of elephant to help fund the Angolan bush war. Today, terror groups like Boko Haram do the same. Gabon is home to 10% of africa's giant equatorial jungle. Teeming with wildlife it is home to 60% of all remaining forest elephants. "
Lee on Boko Haram We've seen indications of Boko Haram moving South, basically prospecting for, you know, we have gold, we have diamonds, we have ivory. Prospecting for places where they can make money to keep refuelling their combat. One of the things Boko haram does is kill elephants to take the ivory to buy guns.
Defending their elephants is not quite the same as doing so in south africa.
Lee Up in the north east of gabon we have a block of about 20 000 square km's without a single road in there. There's a few rivers that you can navigate up in a canoe, but otherwise you have to walk. So my teams are doing one month missions, we drop them off on one side and they walk all the way across the rainforest block and come out the other side. They're doing some of the toughest military missions, probably on the planet, going through swamps up to here, deep in the rain forest
Since 2005 they lost around 25000 elephants to the poachers. But then the president of Gabon, Ali Bongo Ondimba stepped in
President Ondimba If the poachers manage to penetrate this far into our territory and be so operational and free, that is a signal to terrorists that our territory is permeable
Lee The government added a zero to the national parks budget. When I started I had 60 staff and I didnt have a single vehicle to patrol the parks. Now I have 750 staff, I have an armed gendarmerie, an armed police force. I have 150 cars, I have I dont know, 35 boats, five planes and a helicopter
"Gabon's story is echoed by many countries – estimates show a 30% total decline in populations since 2007.
Since 1989 all elephants were on Appendix1, but in the 1997 the Southern ellies were downlisted to Appendix 2, allowing limited trade in their ivory.
Now with the backing of the US, the North is calling for the Southern elephants to be moved back to Appendix1, blaming the once off sale of Southern ivory in 2008 for their poaching crisis"
Philip AWF We know the linkage between poaching, why the killing is happening, its to feed the demand. You've already opened the market now, we know that it will continue, the experiment has already been done and we see poaching continuing.
The situation for those on the other side of the debate is almost the direct opposite . If anything the South has too many elephants, causing environmental damage and more human elephant conflict. They argue that if the communities living between the ellies don't get some value from it, they won't keep on protecting them. Namibia and Zimbabwe also need money to continue funding their anti-poaching operations and both submitted proposals to allow them to sell their ivory.
"Charles Jonga
Campfire, Zim " We're talking here, a global rise in the illegal trafficking of ivory. What then are we going to be doing to protect our elephant, to prevent poaching? This is the income that our sustainable use programme has been able to generate – pay our rangers, greater coverage, greater number of patrol days and all. And we are not going to be able then to support the protection of elephants as if they're in a zoo.
And so the table was set for the debate. The Cites secretariat is not convinced of the link between the once-off sales in the South and the increase in poaching in the North.
John Scanlon We also look at satistics for other species. If you look at the trend at the illegal killing for ivory, look also at the trend in the illegal killing of the rhino for its horn – it's exactly the same trend. Look at what's happening with the rosewoods, same trend. These species didn't have a one off sale, yet we see the same trend over the same period of time, of a surge in this 2008. 9. 10. 11 period.
And then Tanzania, who were hardest hit in the last few years poaching, announced they would support Namibia and Zimbabwe's proposals.
Tanzania delegate He who does well deserves to be rewarded, not a long or indefinite jail term, Namibia and Zimbabwe should be rewarded.
After fierce debate, the vote was cast by secret ballot and both countries' proposals were rejected.
Suddenly, the northern states were upbeat about their chances to get all elephants listed on appendix 1, especially when Botswana, the country with the most elephants, and who have always supported ivory trade, unexpectedly sided with them.
Botswana delegate Botswana's elephants are currently listed under appendix2. Fully aware of this serious poaching crisis facing elephants across much of Africa, we unreservedly and voluntarily relinquish this status and we support an uplisting of all African elephants to appendix 1.
But matters changed again when the European Union announced they would oppose the US and the northern coalition on this matter.
EU Now is not the time to resume the international trade in ivory. While we agree with the proponents of proposal16 on this point, we do not support their proposal.
"Once again the ballot was secret,
and once again this proposal was also rejected. This means that the status of elephant trade remains the same as before Cites... for now...
But these were only 3 of the proposals at CoP17 – and many other species received increased protection. "
Bongani closing link After weeks of voting, lobbying, and debating this CoP 17 has come to an end of parties to cites has come to an end. The next one, in 3 years time, will be hosted by Sri-lanka. So, have the decisions that have been made here in Sandton saved our environment? Probably not. Will it protect some species from the greed of mankind? Here's to hoping..
John While we were all dancing slightly differently, we're all dancing to the same beat at this cop, and we got a lot of fantastic decisions. This CoP was a game changer.

PROMO's:

10sec Of the 500 species affected by decisions at the Cites Cop 17 in Sandton, the biggest debate was around the biggest animal. But will it help save our precious elephants?

15secs "Terror groups are busy murdering Africa's elephants to fund their operations
Soundup: Lee
Will a conference in Sandton succeed in stopping them?"

15secs "The fate around international trade of about 500 specie, was decided in Sandton the past two weeks
John Scanlon: This was a game changer
But will it save these animals and plants from extinction?"
